1. Non-neoplastic Lesions: FNH and NRH

Big pictureThree buckets: nodules (non-neoplastic), benign tumors, malignant tumors. Non-neoplastic lesions are not true neoplasms: they are hyperplastic growths in response to a stimulus, here abnormal hepatic blood flow (vascular abnormalities).

Focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH)

  • Non-neoplastic lesion: abnormal hepatic blood flow induces hepatocyte hyperplasia (e.g. a vascular defect such as a hemangioma or Budd-Chiari).
  • Most common in adult females; usually asymptomatic; no treatment unless large or symptomatic (then resect).
  • Gross / imaging: firm, well-circumscribed mass with a central stellate scar (also visible on CT).
  • Micro: fibrotic septa divide parenchyma into nodules (like cirrhosis), a prominent ductal reaction, and thick-walled arteries in the scar (drive the hyperplasia). Hepatocytes themselves are normal (no cytologic atypia).
  • IHC: glutamine synthase shows a map-like pattern (normally zone 3 / central hepatocytes; fibrosis distorts it). Highly specific for FNH.
Focal nodular hyperplasia (slide 6) (click to enlarge)
FNH vs cirrhosis (key question)Both have fibrotic septa and nodules. In FNH the fibrosis radiates from abnormal vasculature and liver function is preserved. Cirrhosis results from repeated hepatocyte injury and repair diffusely across the liver and impairs function.

Nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH)

  • Non-neoplastic lesion: abnormal hepatic blood flow transforms the liver into many small nodules that take over the liver, without fibrosis.
  • Can lead to portal hypertension (non-cirrhotic).
  • Nodules are hard to see on routine H&E (note the lack of fibrosis); they become evident on a reticulin stain.
Nodular regenerative hyperplasia (slide 7) (click to enlarge)
FNHNRH
FibrosisYes (septa, central scar)No
DistributionLocalized lesionMany small nodules throughout
ConsequenceLargely inconsequentialPortal hypertension
SharedNon-neoplastic, regenerative hepatocyte nodules, abnormal blood flow

2. Benign Tumors: Hemangioma and Hepatocellular Adenoma

Cavernous hemangioma

  • Benign neoplasm of blood vessels; the most common benign liver tumor.
  • Micro: dilated vascular channels surrounded by fibrous stroma.
  • Often asymptomatic; rarely hemorrhages; effectively no risk of malignant transformation. Surveillance usually enough; resect if large and symptomatic.
Cavernous hemangioma (slide 9) (click to enlarge)

Hepatocellular adenoma

  • Benign neoplasm of hepatocytes; most common in young women with oral contraceptives or anabolic steroids (depends on subtype).
  • Asymptomatic or abdominal pain.
  • Complications: rupture and hemorrhage (rare but serious) and malignant transformation to HCC (subtype dependent).
  • Treatment: surgery for high-risk tumors; otherwise stop the oral contraceptive or anabolic steroid.
  • Gross: well-circumscribed. Micro: cords of hepatocytes with arterial vasculature and no (or minimal) portal tracts or bile ducts.
Hepatocellular adenoma (slide 10) (click to enlarge)

Molecular subtypes (slide table, completed)

HNF1α-inactivatedβ-catenin-activatedInflammatory
Driver mutationLOF hepatocyte nuclear factor 1-alphaGOF CTNNB1 (exon 3 vs exon 7/8) → β-catenin activation (Wnt)GOF gp130 → JAK-STAT activation
Risk factorsFemaleMale, anabolic steroidsFemale, obesity, metabolic syndrome
Malignancy riskLowExon 3: highest; exon 7 or 8: lowLow (higher if co-occurring GOF β-catenin)
MicroSteatosisCytologic atypia, pseudoacinar architectureDilated sinusoids with inflammation
IHCLFABP negative in tumor (normal liver positive)β-catenin positive in the nucleus (dark nuclei)SAA positive, CRP positive
  • LFABP expression is downstream of HNF1α, so loss of HNF1α = loss of LFABP staining.
  • HNF1α adenomas are also β-catenin negative in the nucleus (membranous only) and SAA negative, which separates them from the other two. Nuclear β-catenin signals increased Wnt signaling (oncogenic).
  • Why exon 3 vs 7/8? Exon 3 mutations prevent β-catenin degradation, so it accumulates and drives the pathway constitutively; exon 7/8 mutations only mildly increase pathway activation.

3. Malignant Tumors: Hepatoblastoma and Hepatocellular Carcinoma

Four malignanciesHepatoblastoma, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) (the star of the lecture), cholangiocarcinoma (biliary tree), gallbladder carcinoma.

Hepatoblastoma

  • Most common liver cancer in children, diagnosed typically before 3 years old.
  • Associated with familial adenomatous polyposis and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.
  • Presents with abdominal swelling, jaundice or pruritus; 20% metastatic at diagnosis; with surgery and chemo, 80% 5-year survival.
  • Micro: trabecular pattern with fetal and embryonal cell types.
  • Why is survival so much better than HCC? Children have no underlying chronic liver disease; HCC often arises on chronic liver disease that itself contributes to mortality.
Hepatoblastoma (slide 16) (click to enlarge)

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC): causes

  • Malignant neoplasm of hepatocytes; a feared complication of other liver diseases.
  • Hepatitis B infection: prevalent in males in high-HBV regions (Asia, sub-Saharan Africa), often via maternal-fetal transmission; causes HCC through viral integration into the host genome activating pro-tumor pathways.
  • Chronic liver disease, often with cirrhosis (steatohepatitis/MASH, metabolic diseases, etc.): 80% of HCC occurs with cirrhosis (so 20% arises without it).
  • Carcinogens: aflatoxin (a mycotoxin) and vinyl chloride.
DriverFrequencyEffect
TP53 (LOF)~60%↓ DNA repair → genomic instability; ↑ cell cycle → proliferation
β-catenin (GOF)~40%↑ Wnt signaling → proliferation
TERT (activating)50-60%Telomere elongation → cell immortality

4. HCC: Morphology, Clinical Features and Fibrolamellar Subtype

Premalignant change

Large cell changeSmall cell change
CellsEnlarged hepatocytes with enlarged, pleomorphic nuclei, scattered among normal hepatocytesSmall cells forming dysplastic nodules in a cirrhotic liver
N:C ratioNormal (cell and nucleus both enlarged)High
Premalignant changes (slide 18) (click to enlarge)

Gross and microscopic features

  • Gross: one large mass or multinodular; hemorrhage and necrosis; can be bile-stained (yellow-green).
  • Vascular invasion: tumor bulging into hepatic vessels (key feature).
  • Micro: irregular cells, nuclei and architecture compared with normal parenchyma; may be encapsulated, show steatosis and bile plugs.
HCC gross and microscopic (slide 19) (click to enlarge)

Microscopic patterns

PatternDescription
Trabecular (most common)Thick plates, 2-3 or more cells thick, separated by endothelium-lined vascular channels
Clear cellCytoplasm full of fat, glycogen or water; clear appearance
PseudoacinarGland-like structures formed by tumor cells (also seen in adenoma but more disfigured here)
ScirrhousDiffuse fibrosis intermixed with cancer cells
High grade (anaplastic)Loses all patterns: giant tumor cells, hyperchromatic nuclei, pleomorphism, abnormal mitoses
HCC patterns of malignancy (slide 20) (click to enlarge)

Clinical features

  • Nonspecific symptoms: abdominal pain, fatigue, weight loss, hepatomegaly.
  • Serum AFP elevated in later-stage disease.
  • Multiphase MRI: HCC is hypervascular so it is bright in the arterial phase, then darker than surrounding liver in the venous phase = venous washout, highly characteristic.
  • Treatment: surgical resection if possible; liver transplant if cirrhotic.
  • Spread: lung metastasis is common in later stage (slide; her narration says "blood" metastasis).
  • 5-year survival: localized ~30%; metastatic ~5-10%.
HCC clinical features: arterial vs venous phase MRI (slide 21) (click to enlarge)

Fibrolamellar carcinoma (HCC subtype)

  • Occurs in young adults with no cirrhosis / no underlying liver disease.
  • Associated with the DNAJB1::PRKACA fusion gene.
  • Treat with surgical excision; better prognosis than standard HCC.
  • Gross: central scar (often calcified; do not confuse with FNH); may be bile-stained or necrotic. Micro: large oncocytic (eosinophilic) hepatocytes surrounded by collagen bundles.
Fibrolamellar carcinoma (slide 22) (click to enlarge)
FibrolamellarStandard HCC
AgeYounger adultsUsually older adults
BackgroundNo cirrhosis or liver diseaseUsually cirrhosis / chronic liver disease
GeneticsDNAJB1::PRKACA fusionTP53, β-catenin, TERT
HistologyOncocytic cells in collagen bundlesHighly variable

5. Cholangiocarcinoma and Gallbladder Carcinoma

Cholangiocarcinoma

  • Malignant neoplasm of biliary epithelial cells; classified by location: intrahepatic (in the liver), perihilar (the junction), distal (common bile duct).
  • Causes: inflammatory disorders, especially PSC; developmental abnormalities (choledochal cysts, congenital dilations of the common bile duct); liver flukes (parasitic flatworms, endemic in Southeast Asia).
  • Clinical: cholestatic symptoms (tumor obstructs the biliary tree); 20-40% 5-year survival with high recurrence after surgery.
  • Micro: adenocarcinoma (gland-like structures) in a dense desmoplastic stroma; perineural invasion.
Cholangiocarcinoma location and causes (slide 23) (click to enlarge)
Cholangiocarcinoma: glands, desmoplasia, perineural invasion (slide 24) (click to enlarge)

Gallbladder carcinoma

  • Malignant neoplasm of gallbladder epithelium; more common in females.
  • Causes: cholelithiasis → chronic cholecystitis (chronic inflammation); chronic infections (Asia).
  • Her narration: ~95% are associated with gallstones, but only 1-2% of people with gallstones get this cancer; higher incidence in Chile, Bolivia, northern India, Hispanic and Native American populations.
  • Symptoms resemble cholelithiasis, so it is often found late with liver and lymph node metastasis; surgery only if caught before then; <10% 5-year survival.
  • Micro: malignant glands (adenocarcinoma) with fibrosis; characteristically invades into the gallbladder wall.
Gallbladder carcinoma (slide 25) (click to enlarge)

6. Liver Metastasis

  • Metastasis to the liver is more common than primary liver tumors.
  • Mnemonic BBLL: Brain, Bones, Liver, Lungs = most common metastasis sites.
  • Why the liver? Extensive vasculature with dual blood supply (portal vein and hepatic artery) and a filtering function, so circulating tumor cells readily seed.
  • Sources: colon, breast, lung, pancreas, etc. (any primary). Her narration: colon and pancreas arrive via the portal vein; lung and breast via the hepatic artery (or lymphatics).
  • Gross: multiple lesions of various sizes; large ones often have central necrosis; liver is typically non-cirrhotic (primary tumors often sit in cirrhotic or diseased liver).
  • Micro: varies; may look like the source tissue (colon mets look like colon) or mimic liver carcinoma, so H&E alone can be hard.
  • IHC tiebreaker: Arginase-1 is a sensitive, specific hepatocyte marker: positive in normal liver and in hepatocellular tumors (adenoma and carcinoma); a metastasis from elsewhere is Arginase-1 negative.
  • Often asymptomatic apart from hepatomegaly until obstructive enough to cause liver failure.
Liver metastasis and Arginase-1 (slide 26) (click to enlarge)
Primary liver cancerLiver metastasis
LesionsOften solitary massMultiple nodules
Background liverOften cirrhotic / chronic diseaseOften normal (non-cirrhotic)
Arginase-1PositiveNegative

8. Study Guide Key: Guiding Questions and Feature Matching

Her keyClick each question to reveal the answer from her study guide key. Where the key and her slides differ, the guide uses the slides (noted at the end of the section).

Non-neoplastic lesions

Non-neoplastic lesion vs benign tumor?A non-neoplastic lesion is a localized growth from a reactive, regenerative, developmental or vascular process, not autonomous clonal proliferation. A benign tumor is a true neoplasm (clonal proliferation) that lacks invasion and metastasis.
FNH vs cirrhosis: both have fibrotic septa and nodules. Why, and how do they differ?FNH: vascular abnormalities alter blood flow, hepatocytes become hyperplastic, and fibrosis develops around the abnormal vasculature, radiating as a central stellate scar with septa; liver function is preserved. Cirrhosis: fibrosis from repeated hepatocyte injury and repair diffusely; liver function is impaired.
2 similarities and 2 differences: FNH vs NRHSimilar: both non-neoplastic, both regenerative hepatocyte nodules, both linked to abnormal blood flow. Different: fibrosis (FNH yes, NRH no); morphology (FNH localized with central scar, NRH many small nodules diffusely); consequence (FNH inconsequential, NRH can cause portal hypertension).

Benign tumors

Cavernous hemangioma vs hepatocellular adenomaSimilar: both benign, both can be asymptomatic, both have vascular features. Different: origin (hemangioma = blood vessels; adenoma = hepatocytes); hemorrhage (hemangioma low risk, adenoma higher risk); malignancy (hemangioma essentially none, adenoma can transform); morphology (dilated vascular channels in stroma vs cords of hepatocytes with arteries).
Mutation of each adenoma subtype and why it causes neoplasiaHNF1α-inactivated: HNF1α LOF, impaired regulation of cell growth. β-catenin-activated: CTNNB1 GOF, constitutive Wnt signaling promotes proliferation. Inflammatory: gp130 GOF, JAK-STAT signaling promotes proliferation and inflammation.
One unique histologic feature per subtypeHNF1α: steatosis, LFABP negative. β-catenin: cytologic atypia, pseudoacinar structures, nuclear β-catenin positive. Inflammatory: dilated sinusoids, inflammatory infiltrates, SAA and CRP positive.
Why does exon 3 carry high malignancy risk but exon 7 does not?Different sites affect the gene product differently. Exon 3 mutations prevent β-catenin degradation, so it accumulates with constitutive pathway activation. Exon 7 mutations cause conformational changes that only minorly increase activation.

Malignant tumors and metastasis

Why is hepatoblastoma survival (80%) so much better than HCC (5-30%)?Hepatoblastoma occurs in children without underlying liver disease; many HCCs arise from chronic liver disease, which itself contributes to mortality.
3 risk factors for HCCChronic HBV or HCV, cirrhosis (steatohepatitis, MASH, metabolic disease, etc.), aflatoxin exposure.
Three HCC driver mutations and their effectTP53 LOF: dysregulated DNA repair and cell cycle → genomic instability and proliferation. β-catenin GOF: Wnt signaling and proliferation. TERT GOF: maintains telomere length → immortality.
2 differences: fibrolamellar carcinoma vs standard HCCAge (younger adults vs usually older); underlying disease (none vs usually cirrhosis); driver (DNAJB1::PRKACA fusion vs TP53, β-catenin, TERT); morphology (large eosinophilic oncocytic hepatocytes with collagen bundles vs variable).
Causes of cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder carcinomaCholangiocarcinoma: PSC, choledochal cysts, liver flukes. Gallbladder carcinoma: cholelithiasis, chronic cholecystitis, chronic infection.
Primary liver cancer vs liver metastasisPrimary: typically a solitary mass in a cirrhotic/chronically diseased liver, hepatocellular differentiation, Arginase-1 positive. Metastasis: typically multiple nodules in a relatively normal liver, histology may resemble the source tissue, Arginase-1 negative.
Why is the liver a common metastatic site?Large vascular network with dual supply: portal vein (intestine, pancreas, spleen tumors) and hepatic artery (systemic circulation). As the blood filter, it has far more opportunity for tumor cells to seed.

Feature matching

Text featuresAflatoxin: HCC. Noncirrhotic portal hypertension: NRH. Oral contraceptives: hepatocellular adenoma. PSC: cholangiocarcinoma. Chronic HBV: HCC. Infants/young children: hepatoblastoma. Anabolic steroids: adenoma. Liver flukes: cholangiocarcinoma. Vascular invasion: HCC.

Key vs slidesOne key answer lists "hemangioma" as having both the low and the high hemorrhage risk (a typo for adenoma); her slides and narration say hemangioma rarely hemorrhages and adenoma hemorrhage is the serious complication, so the guide follows the slides.
